title: Embodied Interpretability: Linking Causal Understanding to Generalization in Vision-Language-Action Models
claim: Policy failures coincide with attribution to spurious nuisance cues, while successes coincide with attribution to task-relevant cues.
layout: 2 stacked rows (failure/success), left-to-right, heatmaps with yellow zoom callouts
description: Two stacked gray panels contrast a failed trial (top) and a successful trial (bottom) of a robot arm stacking cups. In each panel, the left column shows Now and Final frames in a cream card. The middle shows the scene with a thought-cloud icon (a red-warning network on failure, a clean blue network on success). A curved arrow leads to a green-segmented overlay. A circled arrow leads to a heatmap, where yellow boxes and arrows zoom into attended regions. On failure, the heat falls on background, texture and shadow, with a red X and the label Nuisance Visual Cues. On success, it falls on the end-effector, manipulator and cups, with a green check and the label Task-relevant Visual Cues.
caption: Generalization of VLAs can be analyzed through action attribution. For instance, in the task "stack the other cups on the top of the red cup", failed trials rely more on nuisance visual cues (e.g., background, texture, and shadows) for decisions; successful trials rely more on task-relevant cues (e.g., manipulator, end-effector, and cups).
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies often fail under distribution shift, suggesting that decisions may depend on spurious visual correlations rather than task-relevant causes. We formulate visual-action attribution as an interventional estimation problem. Accordingly, we introduce the Interventional Significance Score (ISS), an interventional masking procedure for estimating the causal influence of visual regions on action predictions, and the Nuisance Mass Ratio (NMR), a scalar measure of attribution to task-irrelevant features. We analyze the statistical properties of ISS and show that it admits unbiased estimation, and we characterize conditions under which action prediction error provides a valid proxy for causal influence. Experiments across diverse manipulation tasks indicate that NMR predicts generalization behavior and that ISS yields more faithful explanations than existing interpretability methods. These results suggest that interventional attribution provides a simple diagnostic approach for identifying causal misalignment in embodied policies.
